problem: The sentence 'A URL with no port takes the default from its scheme, so https always means 443' is false as written. A written port overrides the default, and Q5 in this same chapter uses https://api.example.org:8443, which is https on port 8443. A student may answer '443' for any https URL and lose marks, or contradict the quiz.
fix: Write: 'A URL with no port takes the default from its scheme, so an https URL with no port written means 443 and an http URL with no port means 80. A port written in the URL overrides the default, e.g. https://api.example.org:8443 uses 8443.'

problem: 'So 3 servers were asked on the chain' counts root, TLD and authoritative but leaves out the resolver, which the browser also asks. A careful reader may count 4 and think the given output of 3 is wrong.
fix: Say: 'So three name servers were asked on the chain — root, TLD and authoritative — in addition to the browser's own resolver.'

problem: 'The whole path is one request-response round trip' clashes with the step just above it, where the browser makes more requests for CSS, JavaScript and images, each a separate request-response.
fix: Say: 'Fetching the main resource is one request-response round trip; the sub-resources the page needs each add their own round trip.'

problem: 'This is why a DNS answer is cached and can change later' reads as a cause that is not stated: caching does not cause change, it delays the change by the TTL.
fix: Say: 'So an answer is held in caches for its TTL and can still change later, once the TTL runs out and a fresh answer is fetched.'

problem: 'Weighted and latency-based answers send users to the nearest data centre' is wrong for weighted routing. Weighted answers split traffic in set proportions (for example 90/10 during a rollout); only latency-based answers choose the nearest data centre.
fix: Say: 'Weighted answers split traffic between servers in set proportions, and latency-based answers send each user to the data centre with the shortest measured delay.'

problem: 'DNS over HTTPS encrypts lookups so an ISP cannot read them' overstates it. The ISP can still see that a device is connecting to the DoH server and when; what it cannot read is the name being queried.
fix: Say: 'DNS over HTTPS encrypts the query inside the connection, so the ISP can see who you are talking to but not which names you asked for.'
